1	Mpox (formerly known as monkeypox) is a disease caused by infection with a virus, known as Monkeypox
     2	virus. This virus is part of the same family as the virus that causes smallpox. People with mpox
     3	often get a rash, along with other symptoms. The rash will go through several stages, including
     4	scabs, before healing. Mpox is not related to chickenpox.
     5	
     6	
     7	 Mpox is a zoonotic disease, meaning it can be spread between animals and people. It is endemic, or
     8	found regularly, in parts of Central and West Africa. The virus that causes mpox has been found in
     9	small rodents, monkeys, and other mammals that live in these areas.
    10	
    11	
    12	 Discovery and History
    13	 The virus that causes mpox was discovered in 1958, when two outbreaks of a pox-like disease
    14	occurred in colonies of monkeys kept for research. Despite being named “monkeypox” originally, the
    15	source of the disease remains unknown. Scientists suspect African rodents and non-human primates
    16	(like monkeys) might harbor the virus and infect people.
    17	
    18	
    19	 The first human case of mpox was recorded in 1970, in what is now the Democratic Republic of the
    20	Congo. In 2022, mpox spread around the world. Before that, cases of mpox in other places were rare
    21	and usually linked to travel or to animals being imported from regions where mpox is endemic.
    22	
    23	
    24	 The World Health Organization renamed the disease in 2022 to follow modern guidelines for naming
    25	illnesses. Those guidelines recommend that disease names should avoid offending cultural, social,
    26	national, regional, professional or ethnic groups and minimize unnecessary negative effects on
    27	trade, travel, tourism or animal welfare. The virus that causes it still has its historic name,
    28	however.
    29	
    30	
    31	 Virus Types
    32	 Map of countries known to be endemic for clade I & 2 Mpox
    33	 View Larger
    34	 There are two types of the virus that causes mpox: clade I and clade II.
    35	
    36	
    37	 Clade I is responsible for the current rise of cases in Central and Eastern Africa. Historically,
    38	clade I caused higher numbers of severe illnesses than clade II, with up to 10% of people dying from
    39	it. Recent outbreaks have seen much lower death rates of about 1-3.3%.
    40	 Clade II is the type that caused the global outbreak that began in 2022. Infections from clade II
    41	mpox are generally less severe. More than 99.9% of people survive. Clade II is endemic to West
    42	Africa.
    43	 Both types of the virus can spread through:
    44	
    45	
    46	 Close contact (including intimate contact) with a person with mpox
    47	 Direct contact with contaminated materials
    48	 Direct contact with infected animals
    49	 Risk of Severe Disease
    50	 Although cases of mpox are not life-threatening, some people may be more likely to get severely
    51	ill, including
    52	
    53	
    54	 People with severely weakened immune systems
    55	 Children younger than 1
    56	 People with a history of eczema
    57	 People who are pregnant
    58	 Preventing Mpox
    59	 There are several ways you can protect yourself and others from mpox:
    60	
    61	
    62	 Getting vaccinated. Check with your healthcare provider to find out if the mpox vaccine is
    63	recommended for you.
    64	 Avoiding close, skin-to-skin contact with people who have a rash that looks like mpox.
    65	 Avoiding contact with materials that a person with mpox has used, including sharing eating utensils
    66	and cups, and handling their bedding or clothing.
    67	 If you do get mpox, isolate at home, and cover lesions and wear a mask if you must be around
    68	others.
    69	 If you are in an area of Western or Central Africa where mpox occurs regularly, avoid contact with
    70	live or dead wild animals.

What monkeypox is: Monkeypox, now officially called mpox, is a disease caused by infection with the Monkeypox virus, which is in the same virus family as the smallpox virus, and it is not related to chickenpox [E1]. It is a zoonotic disease, meaning it can spread between animals and people, and it is endemic (found regularly) in parts of Central and West Africa, where the virus has been found in small rodents, monkeys, and other mammals [E2].

Is it currently spreading: According to the document, mpox spread around the world in 2022, whereas before that cases outside endemic regions were rare and usually linked to travel or imported animals [E3]. The document also states that clade I of the virus "is responsible for the current rise of cases in Central and Eastern Africa" [E5]. Both virus types spread through close contact (including intimate contact) with a person with mpox, direct contact with contaminated materials, and direct contact with infected animals [E4].

Direct effects: People with mpox often get a rash along with other symptoms, and the rash goes through several stages, including scabs, before healing [E1].

How dangerous it is: The document says cases of mpox are not life-threatening, but some people are more likely to get severely ill, including people with severely weakened immune systems, children younger than 1, people with a history of eczema, and people who are pregnant [E7]. Clade I historically caused higher numbers of severe illnesses, with up to 10% of people dying from it, though recent outbreaks have seen much lower death rates of about 1–3.3% [E5]. Clade II, which caused the global outbreak that began in 2022, is generally less severe, with more than 99.9% of people surviving [E6].

Ways to prevent it: The document lists several ways to protect yourself and others: getting vaccinated (check with your healthcare provider whether the mpox vaccine is recommended for you); avoiding close, skin-to-skin contact with people who have a rash that looks like mpox; avoiding contact with materials a person with mpox has used, including sharing eating utensils and cups and handling their bedding or clothing; if you do get mpox, isolating at home and covering lesions and wearing a mask if you must be around others; and, if you are in an area of Western or Central Africa where mpox occurs regularly, avoiding contact with live or dead wild animals [E8].
</answer>
